questions.q: What four factors does this lesson say actually drive severity classification?
options: Business impact, data sensitivity, scope/spread, and regulatory implications
How many lines of malware code were used, and nothing else
Only the attacker's technical sophistication
The time of day the incident was detected
questions.explain: Severity in practice depends on these four factors, which is why technical sophistication alone doesn't determine it.

questions.q: In the two-incident comparison, why did Incident B get classified as critical while Incident A, with a similar attack chain, was only moderate?
options: Incident B involved access to a payment card database and triggered PCI DSS notification requirements
Incident B used a more technically advanced phishing email
Incident A was detected faster than Incident B
Incident B's attacker was identified by name
questions.explain: Data sensitivity and regulatory implications, not technical sophistication, were what separated the two severity levels.

questions.q: How does Lesson 11's scoping work feed directly into severity classification?
options: Scope/spread - one of the four severity factors - depends on knowing how many accounts, hosts, or systems were actually reached
Scoping has no connection to severity classification
Scoping only matters for containment, never for severity
Severity is set before scoping happens and is never revisited
questions.explain: Scope/spread is a direct severity factor, and it's exactly what a completed scoping check establishes.

questions.q: What does a critical severity classification, especially one with regulatory exposure, typically trigger?
options: Legal counsel involvement and a possible breach-notification clock, with executive or board notification within hours
No change in how the incident is handled
Automatic deletion of the incident ticket
A requirement that only the original analyst can work the case
questions.explain: Critical, regulated incidents can start a legal notification clock and require fast executive involvement.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe severity as a resourcing decision rather than just a label?
options: Because the severity level decides how many people get involved and how fast, and setting it too low under-resources a real problem
Because severity labels have no effect on staffing or escalation
Because every incident, regardless of severity, gets the exact same response
Because resourcing is decided entirely at random
questions.explain: An inaccurate, too-low severity call means the wrong-sized team responds to an incident that actually needed more resources.
